idiom_name: React.createContext + useContext provider; children exported as static members
implementation_notes: The dominant realization: the parent creates the state with useState, publishes value and update callbacks through a Provider, and children read them with useContext, so the call site writes <Select><Select.Option/></Select> without a single shared prop - the form patterns.dev documents as the Context API implementation of the compound pattern. Prefer it over cloning children: context survives memoization, keeps keys and refs intact and lets one child re-render without rebuilding its siblings. Namespace the children (Select.Option = Option) so the whole family is discoverable from one import; publish a memoized value object, because a fresh object literal on every render re-renders every consumer.
pitfalls: A context created without a default lets an Option render outside Select and read null; expose a useSelect() hook that throws a diagnostic instead.
A new object (or inline array/function) as the context value changes identity on every render and re-renders every consumer - memoize the value.

Replacing a native select means owing the full ARIA contract - role=combobox/listbox, aria-expanded, aria-activedescendant, arrow/Home/End/Escape handling per the WAI-ARIA APG - which is where custom selects usually break.
Context is not a state manager: two families nested at the same level are isolated, but a global store must not be used to simulate the parent.

variants.name: React.Children.map + cloneElement prop injection (legacy React form)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's original React form: the parent maps over its children and clones each with the shared state merged into props, which patterns.dev shows as the second implementation and which needs no context at all. React's own documentation warns that Children manipulation is uncommon and can lead to fragile code, and the mechanics explain why: Children.map traverses only direct children (one wrapper element hides every Option), cloneElement silently overwrites a prop the call site already set, and every parent render produces new element identities so memoized children re-render. Keep it for leaf-only families whose children are authored in the same package, or when the parent must inject props into elements it did not write; otherwise move to the context variant.
variants.idiom_name: React.Children.map over direct children with React.cloneElement merging the shared state into props
pitfalls: cloneElement merges blindly: a prop the call site already passed (including the child's own onClick) is overwritten by the parent's value.
Children.map does not traverse wrappers or fragments, so an Option inside a div never receives the injected props and fails silently.
Each clone is a new element identity, so React.memo on the children stops paying off and the whole family re-renders with the parent.
The child's prop contract becomes implicit - nothing in Option's signature says the props come from a parent rather than the call site.

variants.name: Platform realization: shadow DOM slot plus form-associated custom element
variants.implementation_notes: The platform's own version, for families that must live outside a framework: a custom element owns its state and renders light-DOM children through a <slot> in its shadow root, children declare themselves by attribute, and slotchange plus assignedElements re-derives order and membership whenever the call site changes them; with static formAssociated = true and ElementInternals, the element participates in a real form exactly as a native control does, which is what makes it a genuine select rather than a look-alike. The cost is that the parent drives everything explicitly: there is no dependency tracking and no re-render, so each change must re-sync the children, and the semantics a native select had for free must be rebuilt.
variants.idiom_name: customElements.define + <slot> registration via assignedElements + ElementInternals form association
pitfalls: slotchange fires asynchronously and says nothing about what changed - re-derive the child set from assignedElements() instead of patching deltas.
A custom element without static formAssociated and ElementInternals takes part in no form at all, so name/value submission silently disappears.
Events from light-DOM children are not retargeted to the host automatically; the parent must listen on the host or query the children directly.
Shadow DOM blocks page selectors from reaching the parent's internals, so styling and querying must go through parts/slots - plan the theming surface.
